overview: This late-medieval label begins under the Angevin monarchy, but the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 separated the island’s political future from the mainland kingdom centered on Naples. Aragonese rulers governed the island, while rival kings retained overlapping claims and names. Some imported map shapes combine both territories after their political separation; this card does not treat that shape as one uncontested state.

periods.title: Angevin rule before the Vespers
periods.summary: The island belonged to the monarchy whose political center had shifted to Naples.

periods.title: The Aragonese island kingdom
periods.summary: War and negotiated settlements distinguished the island kingdom from Angevin Naples.

periods.title: Closer ties to the Crown of Aragon
periods.summary: The island’s government became more closely connected to the wider Aragonese monarchy.

items.text: The uprising of 1282 helped bring Peter of Aragon to the Sicilian throne and began a long struggle with the Angevins. Calling every southern territory “Sicily” hides this division. The island and the mainland could share a royal title while fighting over who had the right to use it.

The 1302 peace allowed Frederick of Aragon to retain the island under the title king of Trinacria. The arrangement did not remove every rival claim, and another settlement followed in 1372. Medieval sovereignty often involved layered titles and obligations rather than a neat modern border.

A privilege of 1283 allowed Messina to choose consuls who handled Sicilians’ civil disputes outside the kingdom. Merchants needed representatives and procedures far from home. Maritime connections involved contracts and arguments as well as ships arriving with attractive goods.

Messina received extensive privileges for its silk industry in 1292, and its trade helped sustain an annual fair established in 1416. Silk connected specialized craft labor with long-distance exchange; the fair also gave buyers and sellers a recurring place in the calendar.

Excavated pottery from Mazara del Vallo and Castronovo shows that fourteenth- and fifteenth-century households encountered imported Iberian ceramics alongside regional wares. A decorated bowl can therefore help trace a trading network, although it cannot tell us the nationality of everyone who ate from it.

The same pottery study includes locally circulated brown-and-green decorated vessels and cooking pots. Kitchenware deserves attention alongside expensive imports: distribution inside Sicily connected craft workshops with everyday buyers. Broken pots can reveal ordinary commerce that royal chronicles barely mention.

Sugar manufacture needed specially shaped ceramic vessels to crystallize sugar and collect the liquid draining away. Scientific study of medieval and early-modern Sicilian pots identifies different production centers and choices of clay and design. Producing a sweet ingredient also required potters who understood heat and strength.

Palermo reorganized charitable care in 1442 by bringing smaller hospitals, including San Bartolomeo, into the Ospedale Grande. The archival history makes this an institutional change we can date. It does not establish that everyone had access to modern-style hospital treatment.

The great Triumph of Death fresco, painted around 1440 to 1450, once stood in the courtyard of Palermo’s hospital in Palazzo Sclafani. Its anonymous artist presented death among people of different social ranks. The painting offers evidence of ideas about mortality, not a photographic record of a particular epidemic.

The Steri palace’s wooden ceiling, painted in 1377 to 1380, turned the room above its visitors into a world of stories. One scene shows Tristan and Isolde playing chess, alongside biblical and other legendary material. A noble household could display its reading culture overhead.

Catania received royal permission for a university in 1434, a papal bull in 1444, and began teaching in 1445. Subjects included theology, law, philosophy and medicine; the first recorded degree was awarded in civil law in 1449. Creating a university required several steps, not one ceremonial announcement.

Latin, the title of Pietro Geremia’s inaugural address at Catania on 18 October 1445: “De laude scientiarum.” Translation: “In praise of the branches of knowledge.” This attested scholarly title illustrates the Latin of university learning; it is not a claim that Sicilian families spoke Latin at the dinner table.

ending.text: The island kingdom continued under changing dynastic arrangements and became part of the Spanish monarchy. The map’s 1492 cutoff does not mark its destruction. Its political history must also remain distinct from that of the mainland kingdom of Naples, despite their competing uses of the name Sicily.
